Fluid Resistance in Surgical Masks: The American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) F1862-00a outlines a standard test method to evaluate the resistance of surgical masks to penetration by synthetic blood. 2. Air Exchange and Breathability: 3. Flammability of Materials: Materials used in operating rooms (OR) must meet Class 1 or Class 2 flammability ratings. Materials with a Class 4 flammability rating are unsuitable for OR use and should be labeled as such. 4. Standard Precautions: These include hand hygiene, use of personal protective equipment (PPE), respiratory hygiene, environmental cleaning and disinfection, waste management, and safe handling of patient-care equipment, linen, and waste. These precautions aim to minimize the spread of infections and prevent direct contact with blood, body fluids, secretions, and non-intact skin. The SARS outbreak highlighted the critical importance of adhering to these precautions in healthcare facilities. 5. Hand Hygiene: Hand hygiene is a cornerstone of disease prevention in healthcare settings. Alcohol-based hand rubs are recommended when hands are not visibly soiled, while soap and water should be used when hands are visibly dirty or contaminated. 6. Selection of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE): Gloves, gowns, masks, and eye protection should be used as appropriate. 7. Isolation Precautions: Isolation precautions are critical for managing epidemicand pandemic-prone acute respiratory infections. These include wearing facial protection (medical masks and eye protection) during activities that may generate splashes or sprays of bodily fluids. Gowns should be worn to protect skin and clothing during procedures likely to generate splashes. 8. Respiratory Hygiene: 9. Environmental Cleaning and Disinfection: Pathogens causing acute respiratory infections can survive on surfaces for varying durations. Cleaning and disinfection reduce the bioburden and inactivate infectious agents. Hospital disinfectants such as sodium hypochlorite (bleach), alcohol, phenolic compounds, and quaternary ammonium compounds are commonly used. 10. Patient-Care Equipment: Reusable equipment must be cleaned and disinfected or sterilized according to established protocols. Single-use items should be discarded appropriately. 11. Waste Management: Waste from patients with acute respiratory infections should be classified and disposed of according to local regulations. 12. Handling Linen and Laundry: Contaminated linen should be handled minimally to prevent contamination of air and surfaces. Heavily soiled linen should be pre-treated before laundering, and hot-water cycles (70°C for at least 25 minutes) or appropriate chemical disinfectants should be used. 13. Prevention of Needle-Stick and Sharps Injuries: Safe handling of needles and sharps is essential to prevent transmission of bloodborne pathogens. Used needles should never be recapped, bent, or manipulated by hand and must be disposed of in puncture-resistant containers. 14. Droplet Precautions: For respiratory pathogens transmitted via large droplets (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV), droplet precautions should be implemented alongside standard precautions. This includes wearing medical masks within 1 meter of the patient and limiting patient movement. 15. Airborne Precautions: For airborne pathogens, such as tuberculosis, patients should be placed in airborne precaution rooms with appropriate ventilation. Healthcare workers should use particulate respirators (e.g., N95 masks) when providing care. 16. Preparation of Isolation Rooms: Isolation rooms should be equipped with handwashing facilities, PPE, and waste disposal systems. Non-essential furniture should be removed, and remaining items should be easy to clean. 17. Donning and Doffing PPE: PPE should be donned and doffed in a specific order to prevent self-contamination. Hand hygiene should be performed before and after handling PPE. 18. Patient Transport: Movement of patients with infectious diseases should be minimized. When transport is necessary, patients should wear medical masks to reduce the risk of transmission. 19. Cleaning and Disinfection of Isolation Areas: Isolation areas should be cleaned daily and after patient discharge. Damp cleaning methods are preferred to avoid aerosol generation. 20. Monitoring Healthcare Workers: Healthcare workers exposed to patients with acute respiratory infections should be monitored for symptoms of illness.
